article_text:
ONE DOES NOT have to look too far to find the defining images of today’s India. They stare back at us in public, like the arresting, belligerent face of a saffron Hanuman, popularised in 2018 and pasted on the windscreens of cars. Or they crawl their way into our social media feeds, like the suited-up, sunglass-sporting, victorious insect in the logo of the newly emerged Cockroach Janata Party.

Archana Hande. The Narmada Fish. The Last Rust. Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai. 2023

In her solo show The Last Rust , Archana Hande turns her attention to older, more revered images. Drawing from Émile Durkheim’s conception of totemism, she revisits symbols in the context of the Indian nation-state: institutionalised ‘totems’ like the national bird and animal, sans nostalgia. To this end, she constructs sculptures from scrap—blades and scissors, for example: scavenged from Gujari (flea) markets organised on Sundays. Fittingly, sickles and a long machchu or iron bill hook are woven together to form the torso and limbs of The Royal Bengal Tiger . The same menacing machchu blade, combined with farming and horticultural tools, assumes a more graceful form in The Indian Peninsula Peacock , which seems to evoke both the subcontinent’s unique geography, and the Ashoka Chakra.

On display, first and foremost, is Hande’s ability to transform what is deemed detritus into something entirely new, while holding onto past meanings, resulting in multilayered installations. For example, in Historical Amnesia , housed within light boxes, she sketches on carbon paper collected from a typist near Mumbai’s Bombay Sessions Court. If the viewer peers closely, they will see remnants of the carbon papers’ past lives. “These monuments subvert symbolic expectations by evoking skeletons, corpses, and carapaces—decomposing and mutating. Each object within the assembly carries its own class, gender, and caste history, embedded within the lives of those existing on the margins of society,” architect and filmmaker Rohan Shivkumar observes in his text accompanying the exhibition.

Archana Hande. The Indian Peninsula Peacock. The Last Rust. Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai. 2025-26

On her visits to scrap markets like Bengaluru’s Shivajinagar Market and Mumbai’s Chor Bazaar, Hande does not typically walk in with pre-imagined frameworks; instead she takes away objects that speak to her, and revisits them at her studio. Many of these objects are the tools of highly skilled workers, thus making the works in The Last Rust a juxtaposition of totemic power and the labour of highly skilled workers across community kitchens, garment weaving, construction and agriculture. The subversion inspires interpretation, provoking the viewer to wonder about the greatness of India and how central workers in formal and informal sectors, invisibilised, unlike entrepreneurs and scientists, have been to it. Beyond interpretations of a more simpler nature, one wonders if and how these national symbols speak to the workers’ realities.

The formation of ‘rust’ over institutions and symbols is an inevitability in a changing society; every few years, a new India forms, like a tree’s growth rings or layers of earth building upon each other. A scratching of the surface, the artist says, reveals what came before. To Hande, who initially conceptualised these works for the 2022 Kochi-Muziris Biennale, rust is a metaphor for the corrosion of democratic and secular values that India once espoused. At a time when the names of stadiums, bridges and even cities are changed to sever connections to history: colonial or otherwise, and controversial deletions in school textbooks have been normalised, rust is a powerful vehicle to convey how outward signs of societal decay point to an inward hollowing.

Archana Hande. Historical Amnesia. The Last Rust. Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai. 2022

In combination with its metaphorical value, the use of rust, at once brittle and abrasive, is compelling. Intrinsic to the state in which the objects were found, rather than an effect artificially engineered in the artist’s studio, it seems to be material and medium, melding together disparate objects from entirely different contexts, enabling them to take on a new, shared meaning. It is to Hande’s credit that something as heavy and weatherbeaten as horseshoes can be imbued with a sense of lightness and delicateness in a work like The Cloud .

By virtue of being sourced at scrap markets, the objects are now living out their second or third lives. In present times, India’s repair economies, from the art of rafoogari (expert darning) to low-cost appliance repair, are slowly losing out on past relevance thanks to a use-and-throw culture taking hold. (Hande is no stranger to this culture, as a documentarian of “rejected gods” in a series of photographs from 2011, where she captures how even pictures and idols of gods are abandoned and dumped in public because of defects.) The Last Rust opens up a conversation about hope-giving repairwork of the social kind, “where a new future can be assembled out of discarded scraps as a defense against despair,” as Shivkumar articulates in his note.

Archana Hande. The Royal Bengal Tiger. The Last Rust. Chemould Prescott Road, Mumbai. 2025-26

It seems to reflect in Hande’s own practice: Weaving Light , a tessellating installation whose surface is made of jacquard punched cards once used in textile looms, shapeshifts across exhibitions and biennales, without ego or rigidity. Or as gallerist Shireen Gandhy recalls of a video taken after the 2022 Kochi-Muziris Biennale: the artist recorded the demolition of her works, only to rebuild them for the 2026 show.

Archana Hande, The Last Rust , 7 March 2026-30 April 2026, Chemould Prescott Road.

article_text:
リー・クラズナー、「ポロックの妻」からの解放──METの歴史的な2人展が示す画家の真価

アクション・ペインティングで時代の寵児となった ジャクソン・ポロック 。妻の リー・クラズナー も、ポロックとともにアメリカ抽象表現主義の発展に貢献した画家だが、長年その功績は過小評価されていた。現在 メトロポリタン美術館（MET） で開催されている展覧会は、2人の関係を対等なものとして捉え、クラズナーの真価を新たな視野で捉えられる滅多にない貴重な機会だ。以下、2人展のレビューをお届けする。

ニューヨーク の メトロポリタン美術館 で今、歴史的な展覧会が開催されている。それは、 アメリカ で最も有名なアーティストカップル、 リー・クラズナー （1908-84）と ジャクソン・ポロック （1912-56）の120点を超える作品を一堂に集めた2人展、「Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous（クラズナーとポロック：過去進行形）」だ（2027年1月31日まで）。

ポロックの影に隠れがちだったクラズナー

2人については多くのことが語られてきたが、これまではもっぱらポロックに光が当たっていた。今年5月にはオークションでポロック作品の落札額が1億ドル（約158億円）を超え、「1億ドルクラブ」と呼ばれる最高価格帯アーティストの仲間入りを果たしている。

また、スティーヴン・ネイファーとグレゴリー・ホワイト・スミスの共著による『Jackson Pollock: An American Saga（ジャクソン・ポロック：アメリカン・サーガ）』は、1991年のピューリッツァー賞（伝記部門）を受賞。934ページに及ぶ同書は2000年にハリウッドで 映画 化され、『ポロック 2人だけのアトリエ』（原題：Pollock）というタイトルで封切られた。同作でクラズナーを演じたマーシャ・ゲイ・ハーデンは助演女優賞に輝いている。

確かに、クラズナーは長きにわたって脇役扱いをされてきた。1981年、美術史家でキュレーターのバーバラ・ローズは「Krasner/Pollock: A Working Relationship（クラズナー／ポロック：制作における関係）」と題した展覧会を企画し、「アーティストとしては二流で、伝説的な夫を辛抱強く支えただけの存在」とする当時支配的だった言説を覆そうとした。ローズは、2人の結婚生活を対等な芸術家同士の複雑で実務的なパートナーシップとして提示したが、それでもクラズナーをポロックの影から完全に解き放つことはできなかった。

一方、メトロポリタン美術館の「Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous」は、ポロックの死後28年間生きたクラズナーに重点を置き、これまでの試みと比べ、より大胆かつ繊細で、視野の広がりを感じさせるものとなっている。その理由は、今回やっと2人が対等な存在として取り上げられていることにある。

展覧会は、暖房設備のないロングアイランドの2階建て板葺き住宅兼スタジオのパノラマ映像から始まる。その映像にはポロックとクラズナー、愛犬ジップ、そして飼い慣らされたカラスのカウ・カウを捉えた当時の写真が重ねられている。2人はこの家で11年近く暮らした。しかしポロックは、飲酒運転による事故で同乗していたエディス・メッツガーとともに死亡し、愛人のルース・クリグマンも負傷。当時クラズナーは、夫の飲酒癖や女性関係から距離を置くため、ヨーロッパに滞在していた。

ニューヨーク や、ポロックが足繁く通ったシーダー・バーから遠く離れたロングアイランドの家で、ポロックはのちに伝説となるドリップ・ペインティングを初めて制作した。下地処理をしていないカンバスをアトリエの床に広げて作業を行い、棒や筆を使ってエナメル塗料や住宅用塗料を垂らす手法で、決してキャンバスには触れなかった。

この制作方法は、 ウクライナ 生まれの独学の画家、ジャネット・ソーベル（1893-1968）の絵画に触発されたものだ。ポロックの最初のドリップ・ペインティング《Galaxy（銀河）》（1947）は、1946年に ペギー・グッゲンハイム のギャラリーで目にしたソーベルの《Milkey Way（天の川）》（1945）に直接的な影響を受けている。

その2年後、絶大な人気を誇るグラフ誌のライフ（LIFE）が、「ジャクソン・ポロック：彼はアメリカで最も偉大な存命画家か？」というタイトルで彼を取り上げたことで、無名の抽象画家だったポロックは一躍有名アーティストとして表舞台に躍り出た。掲載された4枚の写真に映し出されていたのは、絵の具が飛び散ったジーンズ姿でタバコをくわえ、物思いにふけるような表情の極めて男らしい姿だ。記事はクラズナーの存在には一切触れず、ポロックを孤独で天才的な男性として描いていた。

ポロック神話と向き合いながら自らの道を切り拓く

メトロポリタン美術館の展覧会は、こうした神話を覆すことで抽象表現主義の歴史を大胆に再構築し、2人のアーティストの複雑な関係を解き明かす上で大きな役割を果たしている。最初の展示室に並ぶのは、ポロックが芸術的な行き詰まりに陥り、制御不能な状態へと転落していった1950年代半ばにクラズナーが制作したコラージュ作品だ。それを見ると、これまで私たちの視野に入っていたのはポロックの凋落という悲劇だけで、その影から抜け出して頭角を現したクラズナーの輝きは見過ごされていたことが分かる。

こうした再解釈により、1950年代半ばの時点でポロックと対等な存在だったクラズナーが、1人のアーティストとして正当に評価されるべきだったことが証明されている。たとえば、《Bald Eagle（ハクトウワシ）》（1955）でクラズナーは、自身やポロックが捨てた暗褐色のリネンや下地処理されていないカンバスの切れ端をコラージュに用いた。そのため、画面中央の鳥の横顔に似た形の白い部分には、ポロックがドリップした黒い線が残っている。2人が廃棄した作品を取り込むことで、クラズナーは破壊の中から不死鳥のように蘇り、新たな生命を得たのだ。

これは、クラズナーの生涯とキャリア全体を象徴する比喩だと言える。迷いや創作の行き詰まりに悩まされながらも、クラズナーは常に前進するすべを見つけ、ポロックという圧倒的な存在と向き合いながら、自分だけの道を切り拓いていかなければならなかった。そんなクラズナーは、ポロックと出会う以前、アルチュール・ランボーの『地獄の季節』の一節をアトリエの壁に書き記している（以下の訳は岩波文庫『地獄の季節』の小林秀雄によるもの）。

いったい俺が誰に自讃しようというのだ。どんな獣物を崇めなければならないのだ。どんな聖像に挑みかかろうというのか。どんな心臓を砕くのか。どんな嘘をついてはならないのか。──さてはどんな血に塗れて歩くのか。

一つところに安住することのない、気骨のある人物だったクラズナーは、アーティストとして自らの誠実さを保つことがいかに困難かを理解していたのだろう。

2人展のキュレーターたちは、展覧会の冒頭でクラズナーが決して添え物的なアーティストではなかったことを示し、それに続く部分では伝記的なアプローチで2人が出会う前の初期作品を同じ部屋に並べている。展示は、それぞれの自画像──クラズナーはグラファイトとクレヨンの作品（1929～30年頃）、ポロックは泥のような茶色で陰鬱な厚塗りの作品（1930～33年頃）──から始まり、2人がともに参加したグループ展「American and French Painting（アメリカとフランスの絵画）に出展された絵画へと続く。

ロシアから亡命し、芸術家で理論家でもあったジョン・グラハムがキュレーションを担当した同展では、スチュアート・デイヴィス、 ウィレム・デ・クーニング 、パブロ・ピカソ、 アンリ・マティス らとともにポロックとクラズナーの作品が展示された。展覧会を見た後、ポロックのことを知らなかったクラズナーは興味を持って彼のことを調べたという。その後の展開は周知の通りだ。

2人の「対等な関係」とクラズナーの正当な評価

メトロポリタン美術館の展覧会には見どころが多く、ポロックの叙情的で雄大な傑作《Number 1, 1950 (Lavender Mist)（ナンバー1、1950 [ラベンダーの霧] ）》から、1955年にステーブル・ギャラリーで開催されたクラズナーの画期的な個展の再現まで充実した内容だ。この個展を見た美術評論家のクレメント・グリーンバーグは、クラズナーを「この時代のアメリカ美術界にとって重要な新しい才能」と称賛している。

グリーンバーグは後に、ドリップ・ペインティングによってポロックが キュビスム （つまりピカソ）を乗り越え、真に偉大なアメリカ絵画を初めて生み出したと断言した。また、クラズナーがコラージュ（これもピカソへの言及）をアメリカの新しい一領域へ導いたと指摘したものの、ポロックに対するほどの喝采を送ることはなかった。クラズナーがそのキャリアを通じて直面し、突き当たることになったのは、こうした序列的な思考（あるいは「ガラスの天井」）だった。

クラズナーは、自分やポロックが破棄したり、放置したり、あるいは未完成のままにしていたものを使って独自の作品群を生み出した。《Blue Level（青のレベル）》（1955）と《Desert Moon（砂漠の月）》（1955）では、それぞれ青と赤を塗った面によって垂直で堅牢な世界を構築し、無骨とも言えるその要素が画面の上下の縁を突き抜けるように伸びている。これらの作品に見られる垂直性は、破壊と再生が文字通り、そして比喩的にも融合した強い意志にあふれる自画像と見ることができる。

展覧会の後半は、新たな領域へと踏み出したクラズナーの作品が中心となっており、そこにポロックの《Portrait and a Dream（肖像と夢）》（1953）や《The Deep（深み）》（1953）などの独創的な作品が数点混じっている。ポロックの死から1年後、再生というテーマに立ち返り、洗練と猥雑が入り混じった全長5メートル超の大作《The Seasons（季節）》（1957）に取り組んだクラズナーは、性器を思わせる豊かな造形を描き出した。こうした大胆な作風は、ハンス・ホフマンに師事していた頃に制作した木炭画をコラージュした最後の記念碑的作品《Past Continuous（過去進行形）》（1976）まで続いた。

展示室には、その間20年にわたって生み出された各年代を代表する主要作品も並んでいる。クラズナーは休むことなく、次々と予想外の試みを続けた。たとえば、《Kufic（クーフィー体）》（1965）は簡素で瞑想的な絵画だが、そのタイトルはアラビア文字の最も古い書法に由来し、クラズナーが長年文字や線的な記号に関心を寄せていたことを物語っている。《Rising Green（上昇する緑）》（1971）もまた、クラズナーの卓越したキャリアにおける傑作の1つだ。

そして、人物の素描をコラージュしたクラズナーの《Future Indicative（未来直説法）》（1977）が展覧会の最後を飾る。自己批判的で、自らの作品に完全に満足することのなかった彼女は、絵画やコラージュの分野で数々の傑作を生み出した。それらは独自の存在感を放ち、同時代のどのアーティストの作品とも似ていない。今ようやく、アメリカ美術に対するクラズナーの貢献が計り知れないものであったことが評価されている。（翻訳：清水玲奈）

article_text:
Andrew Scott conduz um drama histórico que troca campos de batalha por mapas e previsões, encontrando tensão na espera, mas nem sempre força dramática.

“ Pressão ” acompanha o meteorologista James Stagg (Andrew Scott) nas 72 horas anteriores ao Dia D, quando as forças aliadas precisam decidir se as condições climáticas permitem a invasão da Normandia. Uma premissa que prevê homens reunidos analisando mapas e comparando previsões pode não parecer muito cinematográfica. Contudo, o diretor Anthony Maras tem plena ciência do impacto que é colocar uma decisão irreversível nas mãos de pessoas que sabem exatamente o que está em jogo. Esse nível de tensão independe de qualquer batalha.

No começo, sistemas meteorológicos e previsões divergentes parecem se distanciar de qualquer urgência. Aos poucos, porém, a ciência atmosférica evolui de um assunto técnico para um grande problema moral. Stagg precisa defender sua previsão diante de autoridades que desejam uma resposta definitiva, enquanto o comandante supremo Eisenhower (Brendan Fraser) precisa decidir se confia nela. Avançar pode colocar milhares de vidas em risco. Esperar pode comprometer uma operação capaz de mudar o rumo da guerra. Não existe alternativa segura.

Andrew Scott evita retratar Stagg como um herói convencional, carregando a tensão de alguém consciente de que um erro de cálculo pode ter consequências históricas. Sua atuação funciona melhor nos momentos em que a pressão aparece por meio de hesitações e confrontos profissionais. Brendan Fraser oferece o contraponto necessário, interpretando um comandante que precisa ouvir especialistas sem transferir a eles a responsabilidade pelas decisões. A tentativa constante de humanizá-lo (inclusive na insistência em tratá-lo como “Ike”) soa ufanista em excesso, deixando a sensação de que alguém naquele posto e naquela situação dificilmente seria tão “compreensivo”.

O restante do elenco é competente, por mais que o roteiro não dê a todos a mesma atenção. Kerry Condon busca extrair algo do pouco material que tem disponível, mas sua personagem soa por vezes despropositada, o que é uma pena diante da oportunidade de explorar os desafios de ser a única mulher em posição de destaque naquele ambiente. Já Damian Lewis tem um pouco mais de tempo de tela como o veterano general Bernard Montgomery, mas a severidade constante acaba tornando-o unidimensional.

Maras sabe que o suspense mais impactante reside na espera, e aposta nisso também na montagem. As discussões avançam enquanto o relógio se aproxima da decisão, e cada nova previsão mexe diretamente com os ânimos dentro da sala. A fotografia também trabalha a favor dessa proposta, contornando as limitações dos espaços fechados com algumas cenas exteriores que criam uma alternância entre confinamento e amplitude. A trilha sonora completa esse mecanismo aumentando a pressão sem ser invasiva ou querer forçar uma sensação de grandiosidade onde não é necessário.

Adaptado a partir de uma peça de teatro, o filme preserva uma estrutura muito concentrada em diálogos e confrontos verbais. Nessa transposição do palco para o cinema, algumas sequências soam esticadas além do necessário. O filme é curto o suficiente para não perder completamente o controle. Porém, nem sempre possui material dramático suficiente para sustentar a urgência constante que procura impor, sobretudo quando insere um drama familiar com pouquíssimo desenvolvimento.

Também há momentos em que o roteiro reorganiza situações e personalidades para criar um conflito mais acessível ao público, e algumas reações acabam soando calculadas demais. Quem conhece os acontecimentos históricos pode perceber com facilidade quais conflitos foram ampliados para criar suspense. Isso não invalida a proposta, mas diminui a naturalidade das atuações.

Curiosamente, essa redução na escala também é o que diferencia “Pressão” de muitos dramas da Segunda Guerra Mundial. O Dia D aparece como consequência de uma cadeia de decisões tomadas por pessoas que trabalham com informações incertas. O verdadeiro conflito está na responsabilidade de escolher quando agir e aceitar que nenhuma informação será suficiente para eliminar a possibilidade de erro.

Nesse sentido, o longa também assume com tranquilidade a posição de um típico “filme de pai”. Além do contexto histórico em que está inserida a história, some a presença de homens discutindo estratégia em salas fechadas, as figuras históricas conhecidas e a trama baseada em decisões militares praticamente e você vai praticamente gabaritar o checklist — e isso não necessariamente é um defeito. O filme sabe exatamente qual público pretende alcançar e oferece a esse espectador um drama histórico tecnicamente bem executado e fácil de digerir.

“Pressão” não está interessado em reinventar o drama de guerra, tampouco em oferecer a visão definitiva do Dia D. Sua força está em transformar uma decisão técnica em um dilema humano e construir tensão a partir disso. O resultado é funcional e bem conduzido, ainda que a narrativa não alcance todo o peso emocional de um acontecimento histórico dessa dimensão.

高知県立美術館（高知県高知市）で、「没後150年 語る絵金、語られる絵金」が10月31日から開催されます。 高知の夏祭りを彩る「芝居絵屏風」。蝋燭や提灯のほのかな光に浮かび上がる、鮮烈な色彩と迫力ある構図が特徴です。この独自の絵画表現を生み出したのが、幕末土佐の絵師・絵金（1812～1876）。浄瑠璃や歌舞伎を題材に、人間の喜怒哀楽を大胆かつユーモラスに描き出しました。本展では、絵金の代表作が披露されます。また、その芸術を地域に根づく文化として守り、広めてきた人々の足跡をたどります。高知では14年ぶりの大規模な絵金展です。

本展の概要と主な展示作品を紹介

高知県下各地の夏の祭礼に飾られ、闇夜の中、蝋燭や提灯のあかりで鑑賞する「芝居絵屏風」。その独特の絵画様式を確立したのが、幕末土佐の絵師、絵金です。絵金は浄瑠璃や歌舞伎などのいわゆる「語り物」の絵画化に優れた才能を発揮しました。

本展ではその代表作を通じて絵金の軽妙でユーモラスな魅力が取り上げられるとともに、高知の人々の「語り」によって受け継がれてきた「絵金文化」の歴史にも焦点が当てられます。

戦後の高知において、長らく秘蔵されてきた絵金作品を地域の外に持ち出し発信することに貢献した美術家・浜口富治と、赤岡の地域史研究や文学的素養を基礎に絵金作品の出自を語り起こし、赤岡の祭礼における語りの手法を確立した詩人・近森敏夫ら赤岡町出身の二人の活動をはじめ、近年の動向も併せて紹介されます。

2023年度に修復を実施した絵金の「笑い絵」の傑作《放屁合戦図》《夜這い図》もお披露目。幕末期から現代まで変化しながらも連綿と受け継がれてきた高知の絵金文化を今後も伝えていくために、私たちは、そして皆さんは、何を語っていくのか？その未来を考える展覧会です。

絵金（1812～1876）プロフィール

本名・金蔵。号・洞意など。文化9年（1812）、高知城下新市町の髪結いの子として生まれ、土佐で狩野派を学び優れた画才を示す。やがて江戸に出て土佐藩御用絵師の前村洞和に師事し研鑽を積み、帰国後は土佐藩家老家・桐間家の御用絵師となるも、その後「贋作事件」に巻き込まれ失脚し、町絵師になったと伝えられている。風俗図、幟、絵馬、笑い絵の表現にも秀で庶民の需要に応えた金蔵は、「絵師・金蔵」略して「絵金」の通称で親しまれ、「絵金」は高知県内では絵師全般を指す呼称としても流布した。明治9年、高知市で没す。

幕末から近代へと激動する時代を駆け抜け、鮮烈な色彩と劇的な構図で民衆の心を掴み続けた絵師・金蔵こと「絵金」。没後150年の節目を迎える本展では、土佐の風土と熱気の中で育まれ、今なお人々を魅了してやまない絵金文化の真髄を間近に体感できます。闇の中に浮かび上がる極彩色の世界に対峙し、そこに込められた物語や人々の息づかいに耳を傾けるひとときは、きっと忘れがたい美術体験となるはずです。地元・高知県では14年ぶりとなる大規模な展示をお見逃しなく。（美術展ナビ）

article_text:
Fotograf Harald Hauswald über das Nachleben der DDR, den Generationswechsel im Kunstmarkt sowie Alicja Kwade und Jenny Holzer über die Paris-Proteste: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Montag

Kunstmarkt

Philippa Kelly spricht für "Ocula" mit Alicja Kwade über die vorzeitige Entfernung ihrer Installation vor dem Grand Palais , nachdem auch die Art Basel Paris zwei Tage früher geschlossen hat . Die Künstlerin hätte ihre Skulptur aus zehn gestapelten Steinkugeln gern stehen lassen: "Kunst im öffentlichen Raum ist für Menschen gemacht." Sie solle zugänglich sein, Begegnungen ermöglichen und zum Dialog einladen. Auch mögliche Beschädigungen gehörten zum Risiko öffentlicher Kunst. Kwade unterstützt die Anliegen der Protestierenden, insbesondere bessere Bildung, soziale Gerechtigkeit und bezahlbare Lebensbedingungen. Sie bedauert jedoch, dass Gewalt und Zerstörung diese Forderungen überschatteten. Zwar sorge sie sich nicht um ihr Werk, wohl aber um die Sicherheit der Demonstrierenden. "Es ist sehr bedauerlich, dass Kunst im öffentlichen Raum unter diesen Umständen entfernt werden muss", sagt sie. "Letztlich muss die Sicherheit der Menschen Vorrang vor dem Erhalt oder der Präsentation eines Kunstwerks haben." Nate Freeman spricht für seine "Vanity Fair"-Kolumne unter anderem mit Jenny Holzer , die am Musée d’Orsay eine Lichtprojektion zeigt, für die sie historische Texte von Künstlern und Kulturschaffenden auf die Fassade des Hauses projiziert. Die US-Künstlerin unterstützt die studentischen Proteste grundsätzlich: "Was die Studierenden begonnen haben, war idealistisch betrachtet und notwendigerweise gut." Plünderungen und Brandstiftung sieht sie kritisch, wenn sie nicht mehr dem Bildungsanliegen dienen. Trotz der vorzeitigen Schließung der Art Basel Paris bleibt die Künstlerin optimistisch.

Auf ZDFheute beschreibt London-Korrespondent Wolf-Christian Ulrich, wie die Boomer-Generation ihre Kunstsammlungen nicht mehr los wird. Experten erwarteten, so Ulrich, in den kommenden 15 Jahren Kunst im Wert von rund einer Billion Euro auf dem Markt. Der Londoner Modeunternehmer Peter Simon ließ bei Christie's seine Sammlung versteigern und sagt: "Kunstsammeln wurde meine lebenslange Leidenschaft, bis ich plötzlich keinen Platz mehr hatte." Beraterin Michelle Vaughan berichtet, Museen nähmen Schenkungen kaum noch an, denn "für viele Museen ist ein einzelnes Kunstwerk inzwischen eine Belastung". Sie hoffe, dass ihre Sammlung nicht "in Trödelläden" ende. Kunstberater Philip Hoffman erklärt: "Die nächste Generation will es nicht haben." Bei zeitgenössischer Kunst gehe es noch, bei alten Meistern werde es schwierig, "bei Antiquitäten katastrophal". Für Monopol hat Jeni Fulton über den "Great Wealth Transfer" geschrieben .

Fotografie

Susanne Lenz und Ulrich Seidler sprechen in der "Berliner Zeitung" mit dem Fotografen Harald Hauswald über sein neues Buch "KaDeO" , das Ruinenbilder des einstigen Kaufhauses des Ostens mit Porträts aus Ost-Berlin verbindet. Hauswald wollte mit seinen Aufnahmen ein Gegenbild zur offiziellen DDR-Propaganda schaffen: "Honecker hat die millionste Wohnung in Marzahn eingeweiht und in Prenzlauer Berg krachten die Balkone von der Wand." Heute sollen seine Bilder geschönte Erinnerungen an die DDR stören. "Meine Bilder stören beim Vergessen", sagt Hauswald und kritisiert, wie Ostalgie politisch ausgebeutet werde. Auch die Verklärung des damaligen Gemeinschaftsgefühls sieht er kritisch: Viele hätten sich "am Händchen durchs Leben führen lassen und müssen heute selber laufen". Zugleich erinnert er an gegenseitige Hilfe im Alltag, aber auch an Zensur, Überwachung und Verfall. Dass sein Buch ausgerechnet im heutigen Fotografiska auf dem früheren Tacheles-Areal vorgestellt wird, findet er passend: So könne er die Veränderungen an genau dem Ort sichtbar machen, den er einst fotografiert hat.

Malerei

Nick Richardson beleuchtet in der "London Review of Books" die Retrospektive "Beyond Bedlam" an der Royal Academy in London, die das Werk des britischen Malers Richard Dadd neu erschließt. Dadd galt als aufstrebender Künstler, bevor er 1843 im Zuge einer psychischen Erkrankung seinen Vater ermordete und bis zu seinem Tod 1886 in psychiatrischen Anstalten lebte. Dort entwickelte er eine eigenwillige Bildsprache voller winziger Feen, rätselhafter Symbole und grotesker Figuren. Richardson beschreibt etwa "The Fairy Feller’s Master-Stroke", an dessen komplexen Details sich der Blick immer tiefer festhake. Zugleich durchziehe Dadds spätere Werke eine unheimliche Stille: Die Figuren stünden zwar beieinander, schienen aber kaum miteinander in Kontakt zu treten. Die Ausstellung zeige, wie Isolation und Wahn in seine Kunst eingingen – ohne deren Geheimnisse vollständig aufzulösen. Überall gebe es Symbole, schreibt Richardson, doch ihnen fehle der Schlüssel zu einer eindeutigen Deutung.

"国家肖像馆的这次展出——一系列探讨当代艺术家如何运用肖像画的新展览中的首场——是伍德首次大规模公开尝试捕捉自己的面容。她以前画过自画像，但从未达到这样的规模，从未如此巨大而私人。多年来，她的焦点主要在外部的刺激物上：健怡可乐罐、古董、时钟、陶瓷、皮衣。那些午夜末日刷屏、痴迷研究、恋物欲望的东西。多年来，看她以特写式裁剪、柔焦的手法处理日常琐物，就像窥视某人的浏览器标签页，偷看一个无聊、悲伤、过度疲惫、被咖啡因绷紧的年轻优等生的日记。", "她其实从来不需要画自己的脸，因为她的作品一直如此明显地私人化、日记化。但她还是画了，结果紧张而强化。她采用了同样的特写式裁剪、模糊、棱角分明的构图手法，但现在全是皮肤、嘴唇和眼泪。在一幅巨大的画作中，她一边喝着健怡可乐，一边敷着黏糊糊的湿面膜；在另一幅中，她把脸颊挤在镜子上，让扭曲的倒影加倍。在一些较小的作品中，她的脸颊和眉毛流着血；在另一些中，她凄凉地靠在自己的吉他上。有一幅画捕捉到她正在啜泣的瞬间，双眼模糊，悲痛欲绝。", "这里的每一幅画都是她在回望自己，沉浸在自我审视、自怜的内省中。两幅她小时候的画充满笑容和咯咯笑声，但它们只会让你意识到其余图像有多么悲惨，以及她一定有多么悲惨。从艺术角度来说，这并非坏事（但在个人层面上可能不太好），因为它造就了一些真正出色的画作。它们是怪异、令人窒息、亲密的东西，就像你被允许进入她最脆弱的时刻，就像你在她哭泣中途打扰了她。你觉得你必须悄悄退出展厅，让她继续。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这让一切听起来比实际更阴郁、更感伤。作品中有一种幽默，某些地方还有点傻气。在一幅画中，她用塑料粘贴式怪物手指框住自己的脸，仿佛她知道这一切都有点夸张。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
I t might feel like Issy Wood is staring right back at you, glaring out of every canvas, making hard, uncomfortable, unflinching eye contact. But she’s not. The young British painter is staring at herself, lost in soul-searching rumination. You’ve just walked in at the wrong time.

This display at the National Portrait Gallery – the first in a new series of presentations looking at contemporary artists’ use of portraiture – is Wood’s first big public foray into capturing her own face. She’s painted self-portraits before, but never at this scale, never this big and personal. For years now, her focus has mainly been on external stimuli: Diet Coke cans, antiques, clocks, ceramics, leather coats. The stuff of midnight doomscrolling, obsessive research, fetishistic desire. Seeing her close-cropped, soft-focus approach to everyday ephemera over the years has been like spying on someone’s internet tabs, peeking into the diary of a bored, sad, overtired, caffeine-wired young overachiever.

She never really needed to paint her face because her work was always so obviously personal and diaristic. But she’s done it anyway, and the results are tense and heightened. She’s taken the same close-cropped, fuzzy, angular compositional approach, but now it’s all skin and lips and tears. She sips a Diet Coke while doing a goopy, wet face mask in one enormous painting, squidges her cheek against a mirror in another, doubling her twisted reflection. She bleeds from her cheek and eyebrow in some smaller works, leans forlornly against her guitar in others. One painting catches her mid-sob, blurry-eyed and disconsolate.

Every painting here is her looking back at herself, lost in navel-gazing, self-pitying introspection. Two pictures of her as a kid are full of smiles and giggles, but they just make you realise how miserable the rest of the images are, and how miserable she must be. And that’s not a bad thing in art terms (but probably not great on a personal level) because it makes for some really good paintings. They’re weird, suffocating, intimate things, like you’ve been allowed into her weakest moments, like you’re interrupting her mid-weep. You feel like you have to back out of the gallery quietly to let her get on with it.

This makes it all sound bleaker and more maudlin than it is. There’s a humour to the work, a bit of silliness at points. In one painting, she’s framing her face with plastic stick-on monster fingers, like she knows this is all a bit overblown.

It’s surprising that she’s not had more major institutional attention, because she’s not just good, she’s quietly important. A whole load of close-cropped, dark, woozy imitators have come out in her wake. She’s a market darling, and I think we’ll look back on her in a couple of decades as the ultimate zillennial painter.

Few artists manage to capture the crushing, endless, tedious anxiety, the malaise and ennui of the contemporary western condition like Issy Wood. This is the art of the bored, the medicated, the perpetually online, the depressed overachiever who feels like no matter what they do, they’ll never be happy. And as uncomfortable as it is, the mirror she’s squashing her face against here actually reflects us back on ourselves too.

National Portrait Gallery

article_text:
T he philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein argued that our understanding of reality is fundamentally bound by and shaped by the language we use to talk about it. But there is one place where the Vienna-born thinker’s argument ceases to make sense. “Gay saunas are spaces where language dies,” says Vratislav Maňák, a Czech writer and literary scholar.

With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna, a book that made a major splash when it was published in Czech and German earlier this year, Maňák fictionalises Wittgenstein, who had romantic relations with both men and women , entering a Viennese Herrensauna called Kaiserbründl, hailed in newspapers at the time as “the most stylish bathing establishment in the world”.

“To his left and right he sees moist male backs glistening in the water, upper bodies covered in thick hair and nipples hardened by the cold,” writes Maňák. Wittgenstein is shown to be tormented by his desire, by a tension that on the wooden benches of the Kaiserbründl only a handjob can resolve.

“Although Wittgenstein wanted to solve all the mysteries of philosophy, he overlooked the biggest part of human existence: the body” says the 38-year-old, who teaches journalism at Charles University, Prague.

Wittgenstein, the most influential philosopher to emerge from of the Austro-Hungarian empire, never opened up about his homosexuality. Maňák came out relatively late in his life, in 2017, several years after he had earned a reputation as the award-winning author of short stories. Yet his essayistic travelogue defies a public image of central Europe as a deeply homo- and transphobic, or even closeted region.

Contrary to what the strong presence of far-right populists in the political landscapes of Hungary, Czechia or Slovakia may indicate, Maňák finds queer subcultures to have deep roots in central Europe. Visiting the historic 16th-century Ottoman Turkish bath Rudas in Budapest, a men-only space on weekdays, he reminds us that the very term “homosexuality” was first coined in the 1860s by a Hungarian, translator and progressivist Karl Maria Kertbeny.

Maňák experiences sexual epiphanies while raving at Berlin’s KitKatClub. In Prague, he guides the reader through the city’s past and present cruising routes, including rocky trails above the swimming pool in the Podolí district. As long ago as the 1970s, local gay men held a commemorative happening when the public toilets by the Prague State Opera were torn down and took away flame-red tiles as souvenirs from the demolition.

“Even though gay saunas are a generational thing, and younger people have their own queer spaces, it shows ways how you can subversively reinterpret urban space and enjoy it – it’s a textbook of subtle social resistance,” Maňák says.

Many conservative and far-right politicians in central Europe tend to frame homosexuality and queerness as cultural imports from the “decadent” west, which arrived on the wings of liberal democracy after 1989. Maňák’s travelogue is not the only recent book to question that narrative.

“Central Europe, particularly its capitals Budapest, Vienna and Prague, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, played a central role in developing the idea of sexual identity, as many important modern sexologists came from here,” says Anita Kurimay, a historian at Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania and an author of 2020’s Queer Budapest, 1873–1961.

Her book shows that Budapest has long had cruising spots along the Danube and invitation-only gay clubs in mansions, which were tolerated as a public secret. “Thanks to widely spoken German and French common among educated elites, these capitals were part of European conversations and circulation of ideas as well as bodies,” says Kurimay.

Outside of the medical and legal professions and internal police discussions, the subject was indeed mostly a taboo. But there were exceptions, such as the surprisingly progressive 1908 crime novel series Homosexual Love by Hungarian writer Soma Guthi, in which Detective Tuzár solves the tragic love case of two wealthy gentlemen. Interwar Czechoslovakia had progressive homosexual magazine The Voice, which agitated for sexual reform and published dating ads.

Under state socialism, the decriminalisation of male homosexual acts took place in Czechoslovakia and Hungary in 1961, earlier than in the UK and some other European countries. However, people could still be prosecuted for public-offence acts. “Certain liberal sexual politics under socialism didn’t necessarily challenge gender norms,” Kurimay adds.

In Prague, Maňák’s book has also inspired a new exhibition focusing on portrayals of masculinity in central European art at Prague’s DOX Centre for Contemporary Art . Entitled Andros, Greek for masculine, it majors on themes of loneliness, vulnerability and incompleteness: the displayed paintings show blurred or melted faces of men and the ancient ideal of male body is deconstructed to point where only sculptures of fragmented torsos remain. Each work serves as a reminder of how conventionally understood masculinity loses its contours.

“Masculinity, which society once regarded as the central unit of measurement, has thus lost its perfect profile because it, too, has proved to be incomplete, marked by deficiency and irreparable cracks,” he writes in the exhibition catalogue. Yet Maňák sounds hopeful. “I don’t like to use the term ‘crisis of masculinity’”, he adds. “Because not every transformation is necessarily a crisis.”

An English translation of Vratislav Maňák’s With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna will be published by Seagull Books in 2027

article_text:
Two architecturally celebrated council estates in south London that have been under threat of demolition for more than a decade have been saved.

Residents of Cressingham Gardens and the Central Hill estate have campaigned tirelessly for their homes to be saved, saying the low-density 1960s developments are significant in design and popular with those living there.

Lambeth council argued that the estates were in poor repair and that razing them would create badly needed social and affordable homes.

The plans were pursued when Lambeth was controlled by Labour but the Greens won the most seats at elections in May and now run the council as a minority administration.

They oppose the demolition plans, which are expected to be reversed at a meeting of the cabinet next week.

The fate of the estates attracted wider attention, in part because of their design but also because of the many years of limbo faced by tenants and leaseholders as the council pursued demolition.

A 2022 review of Homes Lambeth, the now defunct body which managed housing for the council, questioned the redevelopment plans, saying the net number of social rent homes to be created was very small.

Sir Bob Kerslake, the former head of the civil service who led the review, said “feedback was uniformly negative”, with residents of estates earmarked for development citing inconsistent policy, delays and poor communication. He added: “As a consequence, levels of trust in the council are exceptionally low.”

Both threatened estates were designed by a team of Lambeth architects led by Ted Hollamby , who championed a move away from tower blocks toward lower-rise housing.

Cressingham Gardens, which adjoins Brockwell Park, was built to encourage neighbourliness, with front doors facing each other and green spaces for play.

The Central Hill project was led by Rosemary Stjernstedt when women were rare in social housing design. It was built on a sloping site near Crystal Palace, with homes maximising natural light.

Martin Abrams, the Green leader of Lambeth, said: “This is a decisive moment for Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens. It recognises the relentless work of my colleagues in securing the future for these communities without demolition. We can now focus on investing in residents’ homes and bringing empty properties back into use.”

Pete Elliott, the cabinet member for housing, said: “For over 12 years, we have fought for a better future for Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens. These proposals end years of uncertainty and put the focus where it belongs: repairing homes, supporting communities and filling empty properties.”

article_text:
Lionsgate U.K.’s horror-comedy “ Ghosts: The Possession of Button House ” debuted at the summit of the U.K. and Ireland box office, collecting £2.4 million ($3.2 million) across its opening weekend.

Warner Bros.’ DC horror thriller “ Clayface ” opened in second position with $2.6 million. Amazon MGM Studios’ comedy feature “ Ali G: Who Iz I? ” claimed third place, generating $1.7 million in its debut session.

Related Stories

'Coven Academy' Renewed for Season 2 at Disney

Black Bear’s animated fantasy “ Wildwood ,” directed by Travis Knight, secured fourth spot with an opening haul of $1.36 million. Paramount’s “Street Fighter,” which led the chart in the previous session, rounded out the top five in its sophomore outing, adding $1.35 million to lift its cumulative total to $5.6 million.

Universal’s animated feature “Forgotten Island” placed sixth in its second weekend, collecting $1.2 million for a cume of $3.7 million. Sony’s psychological thriller “Verity” followed in seventh position in its fourth frame, adding $857,067. The Colleen Hoover adaptation’s running total is now $14.4 million.

Universal’s supernatural horror “Other Mommy” took eighth place in its third session with $576,822, bringing its gross to $6.2 million. Mubi’s “Fatherland” debuted at No. 9, generating $264,083 from 86 locations over the three-day frame with a sturdy $3,144 screen average – the fourth highest average per site among new releases. Including preview screenings, the drama’s total opening reached $415,017, surpassing “Cold War” to mark director Paweł Pawlikowski’s biggest-ever launch in the territory.

Studiocanal’s animated holdover “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” rounded out the top 10 in its sixth frame, collecting $408,089 to lift its cume to $6.1 million.

Meanwhile, Mubi’s documentary “Making Marie Antoinette” opened across six sites, taking $1,737 over the weekend for a $24,355 cume. The limited platform bow kicks off a staggered rollout that will expand to additional cinemas ahead of Park Circus’ re-release of Sofia Coppola’s 2006 feature “Marie Antoinette” on Nov. 13.

Looking ahead to the upcoming theatrical frame, mid-week event programming kicks off on Tuesday with Trafalgar Releasing’s broadcast of the Royal Ballet’s “Manon,” followed on Wednesday by music documentary “Ozzy & Black Sabbath: Back to the Beginning,” directed by Ben Wainwright-Pearce across 100+ locations.

Wide commercial rollouts arriving on Friday across 300+ locations are led by Disney’s mountain survival documentary “Everest: The Other Side,” directed by Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin; A24’s dark comedy “Primetime,” directed by Lance Oppenheim and starring Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, and Phoebe Bridgers; Black Bear’s comedy “Wicker,” directed by Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, starring Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Peter Dinklage, and Elizabeth Debicki; and Kaleidoscope Entertainment’s family comedy “Arnie & Barney,” directed by Sean Heuston.

Other releases on Friday include Universal’s comedy “I Love Boosters,” directed by Boots Riley and starring Keke Palmer, Naomi Ackie, Demi Moore, and LaKeith Stanfield; Action Xtreme’s “Bad Day at the Office” across 100+ screens; Munro Films’ documentary feature “Peter Asher: Everywhere Man,” directed by Dayna Goldfine and Daniel Geller across 100+ sites; and “Pan’s Labyrinth” (20th Anniversary 4K Restoration) across 100+ locations.

Specialized, festival, and international titles debuting Friday include BUFF Studios’ “City of Masks,” directed by Andrea M. Catinella; Picturehouse Entertainment’s “Nightborn”; Netflix’s “Gentle Monster,” directed by Marie Kreutzer and starring Léa Seydoux and Catherine Deneuve; Studiocanal’s “Animol”; and Metis Films’ “In the Shadows”. BFI Distribution is releasing a 4K restoration of Ken Russell’s classic “The Devils,” starring Vanessa Redgrave and Oliver Reed across 25+ screens, and Studiocanal is bowing the 25th anniversary 4K re-release of Richard Kelly’s “Donnie Darko,” starring Jake Gyllenhaal across 25+ locations.

The weekend wraps on Saturday with Trafalgar Releasing’s event cinema presentation of “BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ in Sao Paulo: Live Viewing”.

A statue of Florida governor Ron DeSantis has been unveiled in Tallahassee, Florida, which is slowly melting away to reveal a skull under the Republican governor’s face, reported The Guardian . article_text:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good morning!

An environmental group has unveiled a life-size melting statue of Florida governor Ron DeSantis.

Liverpool announces Beatles projects for the city, including a 100,000-square-foot museum.

The Victoria & Albert Museum’s unionized staff plans to strike across all four London sites.

The Headlines

MELTING AWAY . A statue of Florida governor Ron DeSantis has been unveiled in Tallahassee, Florida, which is slowly melting away to reveal a skull under the Republican governor’s face, reported The Guardian . The statue is a public protest from the environmental group 350 Action and advertising agency Uncommon, in response to DeSantis’s lack of action on the climate crisis. “The climate crisis is one of the top issues facing our planet today. And yet, some candidates running for office still deny it’s happening, and deny the bold climate action that the people want,” said Candice Fortin, campaign manager at 350 Action. The Florida governor’s time in office comes to an end in January after eight years. In 2018, he said “I am not a global warming person, I don’t want that label on me.”

HERE COMES THE MUSEUM. Beatlemania is on the rise again: four biopics on the British band are slated for release next year and now, Liverpool, the Beatles’ home city, has announced that it’s moving the Beatles Story Museum to a new 100,000-square-foot location in the city, according to The Times of London . Ownership of the museum is also being handed over to the Beatles’ media company Apple Corps, who has also acquired the St Johns Beacon, Liverpool’s second-tallest building, which will be used as a separate attraction themed around the 1968 animated musical Yellow Submarine . The project is scheduled to finish by 2028. Paul McCartney has called the project “extraordinary” and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said this is the “kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain.”

The Digest

The show must go on: Bayeux Tapestry tickets go back on sale today. [ The Standard ]

James Bond items to hit auction, including Daniel Craig’s “ Skyfall” suit and Ana de Armas’s “ No Time to Die ” dress. [ The Hollywood Reporter ]

The National Gallery in London is staging an exhibition of art acquired through tax schemes. [ Artlyst ]

London museums join forces for a new South Asian arts festival . [ The Art Newspaper ]

Ancient Assyrian artifacts damaged by ISIL in Iraq have been restored. [ Al Jazeera ]

A Russian archaeologist from the Pushkin Museum has been charged with conducting illegal excavations in Kerch, Ukraine. [ UNN ]

Valkyrie Historical Auctions cancels the sale of a Torah looted during the Holocaust. [ VINnews ]

You Hong-june , the director of the National Museum of Korea , resigns following his misattribution apology. [ The Korean Times ]

The Kicker

FOUR STRIKES . The Victoria & Albert Museum ’s unionized staff is planning to strike across all four of the museum’s London sites on October 29 and 30, reported Hyperallergic . Since the summer, V&A staff have been demanding better pay and working conditions, citing lack of hydration breaks and restroom use at the newly opened V&A East Storehouse. Prospect Union’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, said in a statement that “Prospect members are dedicated to their jobs, and it is these dedicated staff who make the museum the world-class attraction it is” and that the museum’s director, Tristram Hunt, has been refusing to participate in negotiations.

article_text:
Christine Haroutounian’s feature-directing debut, After Dreaming , has taken a long route towards New York exhibition. After premiering at the 2025 Berlinale, the film appeared at some festivals of high renown (Busan, Thessalonki) before finally landing a U.S. home at the Los Angeles Festival of Movies in 2026. Nearly seven months after that , the first New York showing of After Dreaming comes this Sunday, October 25 at Asia Society as part of an Armenian cinema retrospective whose programmer, Sona Karapoghosyan, deemed Haroutounian’s film a “surreal exploration of a patriarchal society inseparable from war.” With this occasion in mind, we’re pleased to exclusively unveil a massively intriguing trailer.

Here’s the official synopsis: “Armenia, before peace yet after war. A well-driller is mistaken as an enemy and killed in the countryside. Back in the city, his family decides to keep his death a secret from their daughter, Claudette. They ask a soldier, Atom, to take her away before the funeral. The next morning, Claudette returns from choir practice to find no one home but Atom. He reassures Claudette that her family is awaiting her at a remote monastery. On the road together, faces and places at the brink of disappearing come into existence just as they fall away.”

article_text:
I asked Ellen Burstyn where a Grammy would go, if she ever won one. She stands up to show me.

“I wonder if I took my iPad off the stand and walked you into my office, where they all are,” she says, immediately reaching for it over a video Zoom. Her assistant, Caitlin, gets the camera turned around, and the Zoom window swings from a living room into a study. Burstyn, 93, narrates as she goes, approaching the wall of statues.

“There’s the Emmy, the Tony, the Golden Lion, the Oscar and the other Emmy,” she tells Variety sweetly. “And then these are all awards, too, from various organizations and people. And then these are my nominations up there,” pointing to dozens of certificates and plaques.

I tell her the good news is that the Grammy is smaller than most of those, so it won’t take up as much room.

“Yeah, it’ll fit,” she says wryly. Then, during the walk back: “That’s the first time I’ve ever shown that to anybody. Nobody asked before.”

That shelf is the reason we’re talking.

Burstyn won her Oscar for “Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore” and her Tony for “Same Time, Next Year” in the same year, 1975. Her two Emmys came decades later, for “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” (2009) and “Political Animals” (2013). This past September she accepted the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Film Festival, presented at the screening of Maggie Gyllenhaal’s short “Flesh Impact,” in which she plays Marilyn Monroe.

This leaves one letter in the entertainment gold standard.

“Poetry Says It Better: Poems to Help You Wake Up,” published in April by HarperCollins, is Burstyn’s personal collection of the poems that have carried her through nearly nine decades, from Edna St. Vincent Millay to Mary Oliver to Rumi, whose birthplace she once made a pilgrimage to see. She read the audiobook herself — five hours and nine minutes of it — and it earned a Kirkus Star and an Earphones Award. It is now a contender for the Grammy for best audiobook, narration and storytelling recording. If she wins, Burstyn, who turns 94 in December, would complete her EGOT and become the oldest person ever to do it, passing John Gielgud, who was 87. She would be the seventh woman, after Helen Hayes, Rita Moreno, Audrey Hepburn, Whoopi Goldberg, Jennifer Hudson and Viola Davis.

Burstyn hadn’t been thinking about any of that. But her granddaughter had.

“She said, ‘You know, you’re only one away from an EGOT. You should go for it, Grandma,'” Burstyn recalls. “I don’t know how you ‘go for it.’ But it is thrilling. I understand only six women have ever gotten an EGOT. That’s quite a special event, so I’m all for it.”

We last spoke in 2020 during the pandemic, also over Zoom, when the Netflix drama “Pieces of a Woman” put her in the conversation to become the oldest supporting actress nominee in Oscar history. She told me then that she loved breaking records as she got older. And even though she missed out on a nom, she hasn’t changed her position.

What she wanted to talk today about was the poetry. Asked what she loves about these poems, she didn’t explain, but instead recited William Ernest Henley’s “Invictus” — the poem that hit her in high school — while looking directly at the camera, start to finish, from memory.

“I read that, and I was just so reassured somehow that the stuff I was going through in my life at the time wasn’t going to be forever,” Burstyn says. “That went into my heart, and gave me such confidence that my life was going to change. That started my life as a poetry lover.”

Burstyn has never been nervous acting, she says. Her first Broadway audition — in 1957, for a two-act comedy called “Fair Game” — got her the lead. What changed her was realizing that natural ability wasn’t enough, leaving Hollywood for New York and studying with Lee Strasberg. She is now co-president of the Actors Studio, and her advice to young actors is the same thing she learned there: “A creative act comes from the heart.”

When I ask whether she looks at that shelf with pride, her answer is surprising.

“I could have done better. There are things I didn’t do that I should have done, and things that Lee Strasberg encouraged me to do that I wish I had done. So I don’t feel like a success. Yes, I won awards, and yes, I’ve enjoyed my work. I like to work. But I wish I had gone into the great plays of the theater and played those more. I’m disappointed that I didn’t do that.”

Everything happens for a reason, I tell her. And it’s usually our jobs, the cinephiles and admirers of art, to proclaim to the world what her work has meant, and how important it’s been.

As for the new “Exorcist” film — Mike Flanagan’s “ The Exorcist : Martyrs,” with Scarlett Johansson — coming next year, more than 53 years after Burstyn’s Chris MacNeil was at the center of that sensation, she expresses dismay. “Isn’t there enough already of the ‘Exorcist’ thing?” she exclaims. “It’s enough already.”

Burstyn has a closing argument for the Recording Academy. “I really enjoy reciting poetry and reading it, and I hope people will read the book,” she says. “But I also hope they will listen to the recording that comes with the book — because I think poetry should be heard.”

title_original: 14 Meter hohe Papststatue in Peru fertiggestellt
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kurz vor der Ankunft Leos XIV. in Peru ist in der dortigen Hafenstadt Callao eine Statue zu Ehren des Papstes entstanden. Das Monument reflektiert die enge Beziehung der Peruaner zu dem Kirchenführer"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In der peruanischen Hafenstadt Callao ist eine 14 Meter hohe Statue zu Ehren von Leo XIV. errichtet worden. Es handele sich dabei um das weltweit höchste Monument, das dem aktuellen Papst gewidmet sei, teilte die Stadtverwaltung Callaos mit. Callao erwarte Leo XIV. \"mit offenen Armen und einem Herzen voller Glauben\", heißt es weiter in Bezug auf die Statue, die das Oberhaupt der katholischen Kirche mit ausgebreiteten Armen zeigt."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Skulptur, die unter der Leitung der Bildhauer Deyvi Wong und Rafael Gutiérrez entstand, besteht laut offiziellen Angaben aus einer zehn Meter hohen Metallkonstruktion. Diese ist mit Glasfaser in Marmoroptik verkleidet. Die Figur steht auf einem vier Meter hohen Sockel. Die Konstruktion sei so ausgelegt, dass sie Windlasten von bis zu 120 Kilometern pro Stunde standhalte."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Enthüllung des Denkmals durch Bürgermeister César Pérez und Bischof Luis Alberto Barrera und weitere Würdenträger erfolgte kurz vor dem Besuch des Papstes in Peru, der am Mittwoch in dem Andenland erwartet wird. article_text:
Kurz vor der Ankunft Leos XIV. in Peru ist in der dortigen Hafenstadt Callao eine Statue zu Ehren des Papstes entstanden. Das Monument reflektiert die enge Beziehung der Peruaner zu dem Kirchenführer

In der peruanischen Hafenstadt Callao ist eine 14 Meter hohe Statue zu Ehren von Leo XIV. errichtet worden. Es handele sich dabei um das weltweit höchste Monument, das dem aktuellen Papst gewidmet sei, teilte die Stadtverwaltung Callaos mit. Callao erwarte Leo XIV. "mit offenen Armen und einem Herzen voller Glauben", heißt es weiter in Bezug auf die Statue, die das Oberhaupt der katholischen Kirche mit ausgebreiteten Armen zeigt.

Die Skulptur, die unter der Leitung der Bildhauer Deyvi Wong und Rafael Gutiérrez entstand, besteht laut offiziellen Angaben aus einer zehn Meter hohen Metallkonstruktion. Diese ist mit Glasfaser in Marmoroptik verkleidet. Die Figur steht auf einem vier Meter hohen Sockel. Die Konstruktion sei so ausgelegt, dass sie Windlasten von bis zu 120 Kilometern pro Stunde standhalte.

Die Enthüllung des Denkmals durch Bürgermeister César Pérez und Bischof Luis Alberto Barrera und weitere Würdenträger erfolgte kurz vor dem Besuch des Papstes in Peru, der am Mittwoch in dem Andenland erwartet wird. Leo XIV. befindet sich derzeit auf einer Südamerika-Reise, die ihn bereits nach Uruguay und Argentinien führte. In Peru wird er sechs Tage lang bleiben. In Callao macht der Papst Zwischenstation an der dortigen Luftwaffenbasis. Die Hafenstadt ist Teil der Metropolregion Lima, wo Leo XIV. am Abend von der rechtsgerichteten Präsidentin Keiko Fujimori empfangen wird.

Besondere Beziehung zu Peru

Der Bau der Statue solle auch eine Hommage an die Verbindung Leos XIV. mit Callao darstellen, teilte die Verwaltung der Hafenstadt mit. Dort war Robert Francis Prevost – so der Geburtsname des heutigen Papstes – zeitweise als apostolischer Administrator der Diözese tätig. Die Skulptur drücke "den Stolz, die Dankbarkeit und den Glauben der Einwohner von Callao gegenüber demjenigen aus, der in unserer Diözese tiefe Spuren der Evangelisierung hinterlassen hat", so die Stadtverwaltung.

Der aus den USA stammende Papst Leo XIV. verbrachte insgesamt gut zwei Jahrzehnte in Peru. Der Andenstaat ist für ihn während seiner priesterlichen Tätigkeit zu einer zweiten Heimat geworden.

article_text:
Archives – October 26, 2016

The exhibition in Valladolid, Spain, brings together 75 works of the imaginary universe of Paolo Ventura: a fantasy game of explosion in potentially true reality. His enigmatic circus is crowded with bizarre protagonists: acrobats, soldiers of the Second World War, balloon sellers, automatons, tightrope walkers, anarchists, clowns, lovers and magicians. In the works presented in the exhibition Short Stories, War Stories and Winter Stories, Paolo Ventura takes us into his world, but he doesn’t give us a unique interpretation. His stories are allusions suspended in time that shift our perception and involves usin his subtle play, leaving full autonomy to view freely.

Paolo Ventura October 19 toDecember 11, 2016 Sala Municipal de Exposiciones de San Benito C/ San Benito, s/n Valladolid Spain

Zijn werk verschijnt in verschillende gedaanten: van een mobiele cocktailbar tot een altaar voor vuurwerk, van geplette colablikjes en glinsterende krasloten tot objecten die door oesterschelpen overwoekerd zijn.

Hij werkt niet alleen met beeldend kunstenaars samen, maar evengoed met modeontwerpers en muzikanten én met kinderen en zelfs dieren. Een plan hoeft van tevoren niet uitgedacht te zijn. Mischa gaat het liefst gewoon op pad en vindt onderweg zijn materiaal, woorden en vormen. Twee jaar geleden ging hij op zoek naar een steen voor de sculptuur in de abdijtuin.

Als hij in korte tijd meerdere mensen hoort over de plek Externsteine, besluit hij daar naartoe te gaan. Externsteine is een minstens 100 miljoen jaar oude rotsformatie van zandsteen in een Duits woud. Het is een plek waar door de eeuwen heen zowel heidenen, christenen als SS’ers (dat is een ander verhaal) veelvuldig kwamen. Tegenwoordig komen er vooral veel spirituele groepen, met name tijdens de zonnewende.

Mischa wandelt er rond en ziet op de tweede dag iets uit de modder steken onder de takken van een dode boom. Hij graaft het uit en voelt direct dat dit de hartsteen is. Hij zit er een tijdje naast en begint dan toch te twijfelen en vraagt hardop of dit het object is dat hij zoekt. Een krachtige wind steekt op en alle bladeren rondom hem ruisen luider, tot plots het geluid weer wegebt. Hij heeft hem gevonden. Onderweg naar huis zegt een regenboog hen gedag.

Zegeningen Mischa reist met de steen de wereld over en schrijft erover in zijn blog Blessed. Rocks . Zo neemt hij de steen bijvoorbeeld mee naar Japan, waar die wordt gezegend door een Shinto-meester. De kunstenaar beschrijft Shinto als een grote voorjaarsschoonmaak, waarbij de kosmische vloeren worden geveegd en de spirituele ramen worden gewassen. In het ritueel wordt er gebogen naar de hemel, naar de aarde en naar het omringende, en wordt een stille klap voor ‘het zelf’ gemaakt. Als dit ritueel nieuwsgierig maakt, lees dan vooral de blog. Dan lees je ook dat ze na afloop pudding eten en vlinders zo groot als kleine vogels zien.

Tijdens zijn reis in Japan ontmoet hij ook Koya, een man die zazen beoefent. Hij vertelt dat er in zazen geen zelf is en dat alles wat aan ons kleeft wegvalt. Hij vergelijkt het met licht, waar alles vanaf glijdt omdat er niets aan blijft plakken. Samen fietsen ze naar een tempel terwijl de zon opkomt. De hartsteen ligt in het fietsmandje. Ze zwemmen onder een heilige waterval, waarbij je wordt omringd door een regenboog als de zon precies goed valt. Mischa neemt water van de waterval mee en giet het over de steen op een heilige plek.

In Duitsland ontmoet hij Angaangag, een Inuit-sjamaan uit Groenland. Hij vertelt over de oude traditie uit zijn thuisland, waarbij kinderen van 13 jaar zich 40 dagen terugtrekken in de bergen terwijl ze vasten en stilzitten. In de steen herkent hij het plateau in de bergen waar zijn vader dit ritueel doorstond. Hij vertelt dat Inuit-meditatie gaat over thuiskomen bij het zelf. Hij zegent de steen en hoopt dat mensen zich erover zullen verwonderen.

De zoektocht brengt de kunstenaar op andere plekken, van Indonesië tot Istanboel. Inmiddels is de steen in Berkel-Enschot, waar deze is gezegend door Abt Isaac. Hij vraagt God om de boodschap van liefde door deze steen te verspreiden en eenheid tussen verschillende mensen en religies te bevorderen. Op deze plek kunnen mensen het beeld bezoeken. Al zal deze zo nu en dan ook weg zijn, als de kunstenaar weer een reis zal maken en meer zegeningen verzamelt.

Fontein De steen werd op 15 oktober tijdens een openingsritueel geplaatst in de fontein in de tuin van de Abdij en de trappistenbrouwerij. Tussen de kassen staat de betonnen fundering die water en steen draagt. De fontein is rond, met een opening in het midden. Stenen bankjes nodigen uit om plaats te nemen. Rotsblokken liggen stilletjes op de constructie. Schelpen zijn in beton gedrukt. Verse bloemen schitteren in een vaas, een kaars brandt, wierook walmt, eetstokjes liggen op een keramieken schoteltje. Metalen kannetjes hangen klaar om zegeningen te schenken. Alle elementen verwijzen naar door mensen gemaakte rituelen die de kunstenaar meemaakte. Ondertussen stroomt het water in een eindeloze cirkel rond in de fontein. Druppeldraden lijken op gestapelde steentjes, middenin hun val bevroren. De zon beschijnt dit alles en het is niet moeilijk voor te stellen hoe deze plek in verschillende seizoenen mensen zal aantrekken en daarmee de sculptuur zal laten groeien.

Stille getuige Het raakt me omdat we in een tijd leven waarin er zoveel haat en vergif wordt gezaaid. Ook onder de gigantische spanwijdte en schaduw van de vleugels van religie. Er wordt aan mensen gevraagd om onzichtbaar te zijn omdat ze anders zijn dan ‘de norm’. Er wordt van hen verwacht dat ze zichzelf uitwissen en klein maken, omdat ze minder zouden zijn dan anderen. Ik heb dit nooit begrepen. Waren de meeste profeten en stichters van grote overtuigingen niet onbevreesd kritisch ten opzichte van macht? Kwamen zij niet op voor de onderdrukten en stonden ze niet op de barricades tegen corruptie, onrecht en machtsmisbruik? Zij pleitten allen voor naastenliefde. Dus laten we in vredesnaam meer plekken creëren waar dit beoefend kan worden. Plekken waar we elkaar kunnen ontmoeten, ongeacht (geloofs)overtuiging. Waar we kunnen samenkomen in alle seizoenen. Waar we even losgezongen kunnen worden van onze dagelijkse sores en elkaar kunnen ontmoeten. Een gezegende steen als stille getuige.

Een steen die over de hele wereld reisde met een kunstenaar. Langs avondwinkels, hotels en tempels. Achterop een scooter in smalle straatjes en in een met regenboog omringde waterval. De steen was getuige van allerlei rituelen en gesprekken. Tussen monniken, sjamanen en goede vrienden. Voor het plaatsen hield Mischa de steen nog even liefdevol vast. Handen droegen nog eenmaal zijn stille reisgezel om deze vervolgens in het hart van de fontein te plaatsen. Daarmee is het niet de steen zelf die heilig is verklaard, maar de ontmoetingen eromheen. Het samenkomen van mensen die veelal langs elkaar bewegen, maar allen aangetrokken worden tot iets groters. Een wens om, ongeacht achtergrond of geloof, samen te komen.

‘Blessed’ is te vinden in de tuin van de trappistenbrouwerij bij Abdij O.L.V. van Koningshoeven in Berkel Enschot. Klik hier voor de blog van Mischa Doorenweerd.

Shows

The Power of 70 Decibels: Lawrence Abu Hamdan’s “Repercussions”

LAWRENCE ABU HAMDAN ’s Z

ifzafa: A Livestream Audio Essay , 2025, live performance and video installation with surround sound and color. Photo by Thomas Adank. Courtesy and copyright the artist and the Barbican.

Lawrence Abu Hamdan Repercussions The Barbican London Sep 23–26, 2026

What makes a good listener when tuning into evanescent events unfolding thousands of miles away? And what is at stake? These were the questions I found myself returning to throughout Lawrence Abu Hamdan’s video installation Zifzafa: Livestream Audio Essay (2025) and live performance-lecture Air Pressure (2022), both part of an event series Abu Hamdan produced at the Barbican exploring aural injustices. A simulation of the Israeli-occupied Syrian Golan Heights with narration unfolding in a chat box, Zifzafa investigates the potentially near-deafening fallout surrounding the construction of a wind farm on the Golan by Israeli company Energix. As the virtual flyby takes viewers across the plateau, audio clips of Jawlani village life and animal activity double as an archive of the endangered soundscape. Air Pressure shifted the focus to Lebanon. Backed by social media footage, Abu Hamdan details residents’ experiences of emblematic incidents during the country’s rapid unraveling in 2020–21, and how the din of Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) aircraft trespassing Lebanese airspace became the score that structured daily life. Serving up earfuls of careful research and trenchant reflections, the works are demanding on several fronts.

Installation view of LAWRENCE ABU HAMDAN ’s Z ifzafa: A Livestream Audio Essay , 2025, live performance and video installation with surround sound and color. Photo by Thomas Adank. Courtesy and copyright the artist and the Barbican (left); and performance still of LAWRENCE ABU HAMDAN ’s Air Pressure , 2022, live performance and video installation with surround sound and color. Photo by Mark Allan. Courtesy and copyright the artist and the Barbican (right).

Among the most transformative realizations that could have wormed into listeners’ ears is that silence is never neutral. For most, the firmament is quiet because the price for that peace is being borne elsewhere. In Air Pressure, the artist outlines how 20 countries have purchased and helped fund arms manufacturer Lockheed Martin’s F-35 fighter jets, with all parties bound to the American company for software updates and maintenance. The exception is Israel, which operates its own software, because it has the most real-world experience deploying the jets and can thus provide valuable feedback. Without making a noise, the 19 other countries benefit. Toward the end of his monologue, Abu Hamdan reflects on how the Lebanese skies fell quiet in May 2021 as the IDF began airstrikes on the Gaza Strip during an 11-day offensive. “In silence, we hear what they are most capable of,” he says. Similarly revealing how the absence of sound is charged, the narrator in Zifzafa recounts how Jawlani activists were unexpectedly joined by the Israeli environmentalist group Keepers of the Golan in their protest against the wind farm. For the Keepers, the goal was to preserve the tranquility of the pristine land. For the Jawlani, it was to protect their community’s ties to their home and to restore the lively raucousness that was forcibly muted when an estimated 140,000 residents were displaced following the start of Israeli occupation in 1967.

Performance stills of RANA EID and MATTHEW HERBERT ’s Sykes-Picot , 2026, live performance and video installation with surround sound. Photo by Mark Allan. Courtesy and copyright the artist and the Barbican.

Directly questioning who underwrites the relative serenity of British life, Rana Eid and Matthew Herbert followed Abu Hamdan’s Air Pressure with their commissioned performance Sykes-Picot (2026). The piece traces the specters of Mark Sykes and François Georges-Picot—former diplomats of Great Britain and France, respectively—whose 1916 agreement carved up the Ottoman Empire between their two countries and Russia, guaranteeing control over oil extraction and exports while seeding conflicts that endure in West Asia today. Eid and Herbert had initially intended to use audio clips from Sykes and Georges-Picot’s lifetimes, but the archivist whom they were working with was killed by the IDF in Lebanon this April. The archive was also destroyed. Pivoting, they recorded the places where Sykes and Georges-Picot lived and worked. Recalling a “peaceful nature sounds” playlist, the trickling of raindrops through a Lebanese cedar on the vast Sledmere Estate—the Sykes family seat in Yorkshire—brings the family’s affluence into sharp contrast with the archivist’s cruel fate: a sickening filler for the lacuna.

As the performances and videos progressed, it became clear that the audience’s pleasure is less of a priority than their discomfort. Air Pressure includes a strategically extended pause that forces listeners to halt their breath. Is it over? Do we applaud? Meanwhile, the backing videos are too shaky and repetitive, the sound at times too loud, Abu Hamdan’s voice too muffled. In Zifzafa , the virtual spin across the Golan is too disorienting, the drone of the wind turbines too grating. It is tempting to take what Abu Hamdan’s practice imparts about the aural mechanisms of warfare and walk away with an affirmed sense of one’s moral position. And yet the work seems to invite audiences to sit with unease instead. What channels have been dialed up or down? What might be just out of earshot?

Chloe Chu is an art writer and editor based in London.

article_text:
Christmas came early to London’s Leicester Square on Monday as Johnny Depp touched down for a red-carpet global premiere of Ebenezer in the company of director Ti West and cast including Rupert Grint, Sam Claflin, Tramell Tillman, Ellie Bamber and Robert Strong.

The red carpet was decked out with Christmas trees and artificial snow while 1950s festive classics blasted out in the backdrop, and if by magic, temperatures dropped, ending an unseasonably balmy autumn.

The chilly conditions did not deter fans who crammed into the red-carpet enclosure, most of them there for a glimpse of Depp. He did not disappoint, arriving in a timely fashion to talk to handpicked media and then walk the fan line.

Depp’s latest role as Ebenezer Scrooge is being billed as the actor’s comeback, after being left out in cold following his high-profile legal battles with ex-wife Amber Heard.

Watch on Deadline

Rumors are rife that if Ebenezer performs well, it could help green-light a reboot of the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise with Depp reprising his Captain Jack Sparrow role.

Whether this comes to pass remains to be seen but it was plain to see on Monday night that Depp was the main draw, with the public at least appearing to have moved on.

Talking to Deadline on the red carpet, West said he and Depp had bonded over a shared love of Charles Dickens’ ‘A Christmas Carol’ as well as admiration for Alastair Sim’s performance as Ebenezer Scrooge in an 1951 adaptation.

´Ebenezer’ director Ti West talks on casting Johnny Depp as Ebenezer Scrooge: “He [Depp] was obsessed with Scrooge since he was a little kid. When he found out about the movie, he was like, ‘Alistair Sims is a huge reason why I’m even an actor.’” pic.twitter.com/A2zFDV8J5r — Deadline (@DEADLINE) November 9, 2026

“I’ve been obsessed with it since I was little kid. I would read it every Christmas, and I was into it because it was a ghost story and then I saw the George C. Scott film when I was really little and Marley really scared me,” he said referring to Clive Donner’s 1984 version.

“I’ve had a fascination of it and a version in my head that I was waiting for someone to make that they didn’t make. What’s also cool about it is that it’s one of the rare stories that because it’s so enduring, redoing it, is part of the charm,” he said.

West said Depp had approached him about the role when he heard the production was in the works.

“He was obsessed with Scrooge since when he was a little kid also which I didn’t know and so when he found about the movie he was like, ‘Alastair Sim is a huge reason why I am even an actor.’ It was a weird cosmic thing where it was meant to be,” said West.

RELATED: Actors Who Have Portrayed & Voiced Ebenezer Scrooge: Alastair Sim To Jim Carrey

Depp confirmed West’s account in a public interview ahead of heading inside the cinema.

“I adored it as a child and to this day I know there is no better person to play Ebenezer Scrooge than Alastair Sim… the challenge is to find another angle,” said Depp, praising West for creating a atmosphere on set in which there was space to experiment with the role.

Johnny Depp talks childhood obsession with ‘A Christmas Carol’ and Ebenezer Scrooge at the ‘Ebenezer’ premiere in London pic.twitter.com/hnRAOiODqS — Deadline (@DEADLINE) November 9, 2026

Not surprisingly, given West’s horror filmography, there is a gothic horror to feel to the adaptation, giving the work an extra frisson that goes beyond past big screen versions.

Ellie Bamber, who plays Ebenezer’s long lost love, that it also remains very much a family film. “It’s still very Christmassy with a hint of fright.”

‘Ebenezer’ star Ellie Bamber discusses Ti West’s gothic horror take on Charles Dickens classic: “It’s still very Christmassy with a hint of fright.” pic.twitter.com/EzT3xoTHKa — Deadline (@DEADLINE) November 9, 2026

article_text:
Zendaya is “Dune’s” leading lady.

Multiple sources tell Variety that Zendaya will campaign for Oscar consideration in the lead actress category for her role as Chani in “Dune: Part Three,” the final chapter of Denis Villeneuve’s sci-fi epic. The move marks a shift from the first two films, where she was positioned in supporting actress.

Warner Bros. and representatives for Zendaya declined to comment.

Sony in Talks to Land 'Battlefield' Video Game Movie From Christopher McQuarrie and Michael B. Jordan

Electronic Arts Laying Off 3% of Employees in Studios Restructuring: BioWare Shutting Down, Respawn and DICE to Team on 'Star Wars: Battlefront 3'

The decision reflects Chani’s expanded role in the story. “Dune: Part Three” is set nearly two decades after Paul Atreides (Timothée Chalamet) seized control of the Imperium. Now a ruthless emperor, Paul must face the consequences of his reign as old allies return, terrifying new threats emerge and betrayal lurks in every shadow. Haunted by visions of imperial collapse and the reappearance of his long-lost love, Paul is drawn into a sweeping conspiracy, with Chani at the heart of its unfolding mystery. As rebellion brews and enemies close in, Paul must confront the true cost of power and the fate of those he loves most. The film also stars Jason Momoa, Florence Pugh, Rebecca Ferguson, Anya Taylor-Joy, Robert Pattinson, Javier Bardem, Josh Brolin, Charlotte Rampling and Isaach de Bankolé.

Popular on Variety

The film caps a stellar year for the 30-year-old multi-hyphenate, who could find herself in contention across multiple categories and films this season.

She kicked off 2026 starring as Emma Harwood, a literary editor who reveals shocking secrets, in the romantic dark comedy “The Drama” from writer-director Kristoffer Borgli. That performance, opposite Robert Pattinson, will also be submitted in lead.

She followed it with her turn as Athena in Christopher Nolan’s billion-dollar mythological adaptation “The Odyssey,” where she will vie for supporting actress recognition alongside co-stars Anne Hathaway, Samantha Morton and Charlize Theron.

She also reprised her role as MJ in Destin Daniel Cretton’s “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” another billion-dollar hit that now ranks among the highest-grossing films of all time.

Zendaya’s relatively brief career has already produced an impressive haul of hardware. She won two Emmys for her role as Rue in the HBO Max drama “Euphoria,” becoming the youngest two-time winner in the lead drama actress category. She picked up a Golden Globe in 2023 for the same role. In 2025, she earned two Golden Globe nominations for Luca Guadagnino’s tennis romance “Challengers,” one for lead actress in a comedy and another as a producer when the film was nominated for best picture (musical or comedy).

An Oscar nomination this year would be her first.

Warner Bros. will release “Dune: Part Three” in theaters and Imax on Dec. 18.
